How To Do It: Place baby face-down on your bare chest at a 45° recline. Get face-to-face: your face is their strongest motivation to lift their head.
Materials Required: A reclined chair, couch, or pillows to prop yourself up

How To Do It: Lay baby face-down on a firm, clean surface. Place a rolled muslin under chest to ease the lift. Start 2 min and add 1 min per week.
Lay baby on back; hold ankles gently and move legs in slow cycling motions. Say 'pedal, pedal' rhythmically while maintaining eye contact.
Gently hold baby's forearms, slowly extend arms outward, then bring hands together at midline over chest. Repeat 5 times each side.
Hold a high-contrast B&W card 25 cm from baby's face. Move it slowly left then right. Let eyes find it before you move again.
Hold baby upright against your shoulder and let them practice holding their head for 10–15 seconds. Support gently: don't grip.
Hold a light scarf 15 cm above baby's feet while they lie on back. Let them discover kicking makes it move: first cause-effect feedback.
Place baby on their side with a rolled towel tucked behind their back for support. Alternate sides each session; 5 min per side.
Place your index finger in baby's palm and let the grasp reflex close around it. Gently tug to stimulate the grip.
With warm hands make small circular motions across each palm and each finger. Open fisted hands gently with thumb-stroke wrist to fingertips.
When baby's fists are clenched, gently stroke from wrist to fingertips along the back of the hand to encourage opening.
Gently bring baby's hands together at the centre of their chest. Hold 3 seconds, release. This builds bilateral brain coordination.
Hold baby's forearm steady and gently rotate the wrist in small circles, 5 times each direction on each hand.
Place a small rolled cloth in baby's palm. Note how long the grasp reflex holds it and whether they bring it toward their mouth.
Talk through every nappy change, feed, and bath. 'Now I'm lifting your legs. This might feel cool.' Tone matters more than words.
Sing one consistent song at the same time each day. Repetition builds a neural safety pattern. Same song, same voice, every day.
When baby makes any vowel sound, mirror it back exactly. Pause 10 full seconds before speaking again: that gap is the lesson.
After speaking or making a sound, count to 10 silently before responding again. You are teaching conversation structure.
Call baby's name from 1 metre away (not from directly in front). Watch for eyes or head turning toward the sound.
Introduce one new household sound daily: wooden spoon on pot, rustling paper, running water. Watch how baby stills and locates.
Use a slightly higher pitch and slower pace than normal when talking to baby. This is biologically optimal for infant language processing.
Read any book, recipe, or message aloud to baby. The vocabulary range and rhythm matter: comprehension is irrelevant at this stage.
Hold a black-and-white card 25 cm from baby's face. Let them fixate 10 seconds before moving slowly left. Newborn vision peaks at this distance.
Hold your face 20–30 cm from baby's. Make one slow exaggerated expression and hold it. Wait 10 seconds for their response.
Hold a small unbreakable mirror 25 cm from baby. They won't recognise themselves yet, but the responsive face is deeply engaging.
Cover your face with your hands. Hold 3 seconds. Reveal warmly. Very early object permanence and social anticipation practice.
Carry baby toward a window or lamp. Let them observe light change as you move closer and further. Narrate: 'Bright! Now darker.'
Hold a high-contrast picture book 25 cm from baby. Spend 20–30 seconds on each page before turning. One page can hold attention this age.
Undress baby to nappy and hold against bare chest tummy-to-tummy. Cover both lightly. Regulates temperature, cortisol, and heart rate.
When baby makes a mouth movement or social smile, reflect it back immediately and wait. You are teaching: my expression has social power.
When baby cries, respond before escalation. Consistent early response builds the secure attachment base for all future relationships.
Name what you see: 'You look uncomfortable. Let me see what's wrong.' Labelling emotional states builds the circuits for self-regulation later.
Let each main caregiver hold baby skin-to-skin. Each person's unique warmth and heartbeat is a distinct and valuable regulatory experience.
When you feel anxious, slow your own breathing while holding baby. They sense and entrain to your nervous system state.
Warm oil in palms. Begin with legs: least sensitive. Long slow strokes hip to foot, then arms, back, head. Stimulates vagus nerve.
Gently touch different textures to baby's palm and feet: soft cloth, smooth wood, cool spoon. Name each: 'Soft. Smooth. Cool.'
Take baby outside for 10–15 min. Wind, natural light, birdsong, and temperature variation are multi-sensory inputs no indoor space can replicate.
During bath, pour water at slightly different temperatures on hands. Narrate: 'Warm water now. A little cooler.'
Place baby against your chest and hum or sing. The physical vibration is felt across their whole body and is deeply calming.
Learn early hunger cues: rooting, hand-to-mouth, stirring. Feed before crying. Responding to early cues builds baby's signal-response trust.
Track awake time: 0–6 weeks = 45–60 min; 6–12 weeks = 60–90 min. Beginning sleep routine before overtiredness sets in improves settling.
Place an interesting toy just out of reach during tummy time. The motivation to lift and reach makes effort more sustained.
In tummy time, gently rock baby's hips toward one side. Give the nervous system the sensation of weight transfer needed for rolling.
Place baby on their back. Gently cross one leg over the other and let momentum encourage rolling to the side. Celebrate any attempt.
Sit baby on your lap facing outward, hands loosely around their trunk. Let them feel the work: don't over-support.
In tummy time, once baby pushes up on forearms, gently rock their hips side to side. This is the direct predecessor of rolling.
Hold your palms against baby's feet while they lie on back. Let them push: this activates leg extensors used later for standing.
Hold baby upright on your lap, supporting under arms, and let them bounce slightly. Vestibular input and leg strength combined.
Prop an unbreakable mirror in front of baby during tummy time. Their own face is one of the strongest motivators to lift the head.
Hang a lightweight object (cloth, spoon) just above baby's chest while they lie on back. Wait: let them discover swiping makes it move.
Materials Required: Cloth, ribbon, or spoon on string

How To Do It: Offer a toy wider than one hand. Watch whether they use both hands together: bilateral integration milestone appearing around 4–5 months.
Give a toy in one hand, then offer a second near the other. Do they transfer the first, or hold both? Transfer appears around 5–6 months.
Hand baby a small container with dried lentils inside. Let them discover shaking makes sound: first voluntary cause-effect action.
Give a piece of crinkled paper or foil (supervised). The sound, texture, and visual feedback engage three senses simultaneously.
Press a textured surface gently against baby's palm: a mesh bag, rough towel, smooth cup. The hand's sensory map is being built now.
When baby coos or babbles, echo it back exactly. Then add one new syllable: 'ooh… and then… ba?' Pause 10 seconds each time.
Try raspberry sounds, sudden peekaboo, lifting gently in the air. The belly laugh (appearing around 3–4 months) is a major milestone.
Model ba-ba-ba, ma-ma-ma, da-da-da during alert windows. These are the first consonants baby will produce at 5–6 months.
Speak in two languages fluidly during routines. 'Now we're washing your hands: haath dho rahe hain.' Bilingual input from birth is a gift.
Point to each family member and say their name slowly. 'This is Dadi. Dadi.' Repetition over weeks builds face-name recognition.
Play a different musical genre each day this week: classical, folk, jazz, film songs. Varied sound builds auditory discrimination.
Call baby's name from different positions: behind, left, right. Turn-to-name appearing consistently by 6 months is a key milestone.
Sing a familiar song and stop mid-verse. Wait. Watch baby's face: anticipation appearing means they have learned the pattern.
While baby watches, slowly hide your face behind a cloth or book. Wait 5 seconds. Reveal. Object permanence for faces is appearing now.
Give baby a rattle. Let them discover that shaking = sound. When they look surprised after shaking, they have understood cause-effect.
Materials Required: Rattle or sealed container with lentils

How To Do It: Show baby how to put an object into a bowl and take it out. Let them try. In-out schema is foundational for spatial reasoning.
Point at objects and then look at baby's face: do they follow your point? Joint attention developing around 5–6 months.
Give two very different textures simultaneously: smooth and rough. Let baby feel both and switch between them. Comparison is the lesson.
Do an action three times that baby enjoys: a raspberry, a bounce. On the fourth, pause before. Watch for anticipatory smile.
Every time baby smiles, reflect it back immediately with warmth. Teaching: my positive emotion has social power. This builds communication.
When a new person is present, hold baby and engage the person warmly yourself. Baby reads your calm as: this person is safe.
When baby shows displeasure at a game stopping, restart it. Teaching: expressing a feeling produces a response. Foundation of communication.
Step out of baby's visual field for 30 seconds. Return before they cry. Gradually extend. Teaching: the person comes back.
Name emotions you see: 'You love that sound! Your face lit up.' Accurate emotional labelling builds the brain's emotional vocabulary.
Hold up an interesting object and look between it and baby's face: object, baby, object. This is joint attention, a language precursor.
Let baby kick freely in the bath for 5 extra minutes. Water resistance builds leg strength while providing rich sensory feedback.
Walk outside slowly, narrating each sensory experience: 'That's wind on your face. Listen: that's a crow.' Multi-sensory saturation.
If starting solids, introduce one very smooth purée at a time. Oral sensory exploration (taste and texture together) is its own skill.
Hold baby and sway or dance to music with rhythm. Vestibular input plus auditory rhythm is two systems activating simultaneously.
Alternate placing a cool and slightly warm cloth against baby's hands. Narrate each change. Temperature discrimination is developing.
Establish a consistent pre-feed sequence (dim lights, hold position, a specific phrase). Predictability regulates baby's anticipatory state.
Same 3–4 steps before every nap: swaddle/sleep sack, darken room, white noise, feed. Consistent cues train the brain to prepare for sleep.
Sit baby on firm surface. Place a toy slightly to the side so they must lean to reach. Each topple-and-catch is a core strength exercise.
Place a desirable toy 50 cm in front of baby on the floor. Stay beside or behind (not in front) so they crawl away from you.
Place baby on hands and knees (support if needed). Place a toy just out of reach. Watch for rocking: the crawl motor pattern loading.
Place a rolled blanket or sofa cushion in the crawl path. Watch whether baby navigates around or over it. Motor problem-solving.
Position baby next to a stable low piece of furniture. Place a toy on the surface above their head. Support at hips, not hands.
Place a toy at 45° from baby in tummy time. Watch them pivot their body to follow. This uses the same muscles as crawling.
Hold both of baby's hands from behind and let them walk forward at their own pace. Alternate to one hand as confidence grows.
Let baby crawl up 2–3 safe stairs with you directly behind. Stair climbing builds strength, coordination, and spatial awareness.
Place large puffed snacks or safe small objects on a tray. Watch how they pick up: raking grasp transitioning to pincer grasp.
Materials Required: Puffed snack or small safe object

How To Do It: Give a large container and 4–5 objects. Let baby drop them in and dump them out repeatedly. Foundational spatial reasoning.
Give two objects and demonstrate banging them together. When baby copies, bilateral motor coordination and cause-effect are both working.
Offer a board book and let baby try to turn pages. Even clumsy turning is fine motor skill and book engagement combined.
Stack 2 blocks, let baby knock them over. The knock is as developmental as the build: cause-effect with a satisfying outcome.
Show baby how to move an object from one bowl to another. This requires spatial planning and goal-directed motor action.
When baby produces ba-ba, da-da, or ma-ma, echo immediately and expand: 'Ba ba ba! And then: da da da?' Pause 10 seconds.
Test: call baby's name from 2 m away in a normal voice. Consistent response by 9 months is a key language milestone.
Wave goodbye every single time anyone leaves. Every time, consistently. First gestural communication appears 8–10 months.
Point at objects throughout the day and name them. When baby points at something, immediately name it and comment.
Board book: point to each picture, name it, wait 5 seconds. 'Woh kya hai? Haan: aam! Mango. Peela aam.' Dual-language counts.
Use consistent simple instructions with gesture: 'Come here' + open arms. 'Give me' + open hand. Gesture + word together.
Record 2 minutes of serve-and-return babble conversation. Listen back: count how many turns baby takes. Target: 3+ by 9 months.
Touch each body part and name it while bathing or dressing. 'Yeh naak hai. Yeh haath.' Touch plus name = dual encoding.
Show baby an interesting toy. While they watch, hide it under a cloth. Say 'Kahaan gayi?' Watch whether they search under the cloth.
Place a toy on a cloth, toy out of reach but cloth within reach. Watch if baby pulls the cloth to get the toy: means-ends planning.
Any toy that produces a response when pressed or moved. Systematic testing of what each element does is emerging scientific method.
Offer objects in two distinct sizes. Watch how baby handles them differently: size discrimination precedes sorting by months.
Tap a surface, shake your head, clap: do a simple action and wait. Imitation of familiar actions appears around 8–9 months.
Let baby see you hide an object under one of two cups. Which cup do they look under? Tracking invisible displacement is developing.
When baby shows anxiety with new people, hold them securely and engage the stranger warmly. Don't force contact: baby reads your calm.
When baby clearly communicates 'no more' (turns away, arches), stop immediately. Teaching: your communication is respected.
Leave baby with a known caregiver for 10–15 min. Return before distress. Consistent returns build the trust that makes separations easier.
Sit in front of a large mirror with baby. Point to their reflection, then yours. 'Kaun hai yeh? Tum ho!' Social-cognitive learning.
Find 3 things that reliably make baby laugh. Do them daily. The belly laugh is a major social-emotional development marker.
Call 'Where's Papa?' when Papa is out of sight. Watch baby look toward the right location. Person permanence = secure attachment working.
Let baby crawl on different surfaces: carpet, smooth floor, grass, a mat outside. Each surface is different proprioceptive input.
Extended bath time: 15 min. Let baby splash, pour, and explore. Water provides resistance, temperature, visual, and auditory input simultaneously.
Outdoors: let baby touch bark, leaves, stones, soil (if safe). Natural textures are the richest sensory input available.
At this age, mouthing is the primary sensory tool. Provide safe, clean objects of varied size and texture. Don't interrupt unless unsafe.
Materials Required: Safe household objects of varied texture

How To Do It: Make an interesting sound from behind baby, left, right, and above. Watch how accurately they turn toward each direction.
Give baby a spoon during feeding. Messy self-feeding attempts (however unsuccessful) build fine motor and self-care simultaneously.
Offer a small open cup with a tiny amount of water. Supervised sipping: not for intake, for the skill of cup management.
Place a toy at the far end of the sofa. Baby learns to step sideways while holding on: each step is a walking lesson.
Sit 1–2 steps from furniture baby is holding. Open arms and call their name. Close the gap gradually as confidence grows.
While baby stands holding furniture, catch their attention from the other side. Count the independent standing seconds each day.
With you directly behind, let baby learn to descend stairs backwards (feet first). This is safer than forward and builds spatial awareness.
Roll a large soft ball toward baby's feet while they stand with support. Kicking combines balance, timing, and motor planning.
Ask baby to carry a lightweight object while walking (holding your hand). Dual-task walking builds automaticity.
Give baby a push-along toy (cardboard box works) to push while walking. The resistance helps them control speed and direction.
Walk on grass, gravel path, or slight slope with one hand held. Variable terrain builds adaptive balance faster than smooth floors.
Offer small safe objects on a tray. A precise thumb-index pincer grip developing by 12 months is a fine motor milestone.
Hold a crayon with baby's hand and make marks on paper. The first deliberate mark (even if uncontrolled) is the beginning of writing.
Demonstrate stacking 2 blocks then hand one to baby. Can they place it on top? 2-block tower by 12 months = spatial milestone.
Cut a slot in a box lid and provide objects that fit through. Posting requires visual-spatial matching: demanding for this age.
Let baby turn board book pages. Even turning multiple at once counts: the intent to turn is the milestone, not the accuracy.
Offer a large-lidded container. Show loosening a lid; let them try. Rotation movements are a distinct fine motor skill.
When they say 'mama' or 'dada' directed at the correct person, respond warmly and immediately. First true words are emerging now.
This week, note every consistent sound used to mean a specific thing. 'ba' always for ball = a first word even if it doesn't sound adult.
When baby says one word, add two: 'ba' → 'ball! Big red ball.' Every expansion teaches: what you said has a more complete version.
Wave bye-bye every single time anyone leaves. First spontaneous contextual wave (not prompted) marks true gestural communication.
Every time baby points, immediately name what they're pointing at and comment. The point deserves a full response, every time.
Come here' / 'Give me' / 'Where is the ball?' with consistent gesture. Following 1-step instructions by 12 months is a key milestone.
Sing rhymes with hand actions: 'taalee bajao', 'Johny Johny'. Baby learns to do the actions before saying the words.
During bath or dressing, ask 'Kahaan hai naak?' and point. Recognising 2–3 body parts on command by 12 months is typical.
Hide a toy under one of two cloths while baby watches. Do they search the correct one? Searching correctly = solid object permanence.
Hand baby a cloth when you wipe a surface. Give them a spoon when you stir. They imitate because they understand the action's purpose.
A 2-piece puzzle (shape fits a hole) shows visual discrimination, spatial rotation awareness, and persistence.
Show baby the toy going under one cup. Reverse the cup with the toy and ask: where did it go? Object-tracking in 3D space.
Pretend to drink from an empty cup, or put a toy phone to your ear. When baby imitates: symbolic thought has arrived.
Put a favourite toy in a closed (not locked) box. Watch what baby does to open it: persistence and problem-solving combined.
Note whether baby initiates affection: reaches up to be held, hugs, brings you objects. These are attachment behaviours to celebrate.
When baby deliberately drops something and watches your reaction: they are testing social rules. Calm, consistent responses are the lesson.
If someone nearby is crying or upset, narrate what you see: 'Woh reh rahi hai. Shayad dukh lag raha hai use.' Early empathy wiring.
Leave for a consistent 15–20 minute trip. Confident goodbye + return as promised + warmth on return = secure separation learning.
Arrange play near another baby. No expectation of interaction: parallel play beside another child is the correct stage right now.
Repeat a social game (peek-a-boo, tickle, bounce) and stop mid-way. Watch baby signal for continuation: communication is purposeful.
Fill a shallow container with dry rice or lentils. Let baby scoop, pour, and run hands through. Supervised closely.
Let baby crawl or stand on grass, sand, or mud (if safe). The resistance and texture of outdoor ground is uniquely rich input.
Hold baby and move to music with a clear beat. Note what genres they respond to: musical personality is forming.
Roll baby gently in a blanket, lift in air briefly, spin slowly. Vestibular system thrives on varied whole-body movement.
Puréed food or yoghurt on a tray. Let baby touch, smear, and explore. Tactile tolerance built now prevents later sensory avoidance.
Baby-led spoon feeding: messy and slow is correct. The independence matters more than the quantity eaten.
Let baby try to remove their own socks. This develops fine motor skill and body-care independence simultaneously.
Daily outdoor walking on grass, gravel, or slopes builds adaptive balance far faster than smooth indoor floors.
Let baby climb on and off a sofa cushion on the floor under supervision. Climbing builds shoulder, core, and spatial judgement.
Place toys on the floor and encourage baby to squat to retrieve them instead of bending at the waist. Squat builds hip and core strength.
Roll a large soft ball toward baby and encourage kicking. Timing, balance on one foot, and motor planning combine in this action.
Demonstrate overhead throwing and let baby try. Even wild attempts build the shoulder rotation and release control needed for throwing.
Ask baby to carry a lightweight object from one room to another. Dual-task locomotion shows walking is becoming automatic.
Put on music and dance together. Free movement to music builds coordination, rhythm, and body awareness simultaneously.
Practice going up and down stairs with one hand held. By 15 months most children can navigate with support.
Large crayons on big paper. Any mark is the goal: this is the beginning of all future writing. Celebrate every mark.
Stack 4 blocks and let baby copy. Knock down and restart. 4-block tower by 15 months is solid fine motor development.
Start with just the circular hole: no rotation needed. Success with circle before introducing shapes that require rotation.
Thread large beads or pasta onto a thick cord. Requires two-hand coordination, visual targeting, and sustained attention.
Water play with two containers: fill one, pour into other. The control of pouring is a fine motor skill used in self-care for years.
Place large stickers on paper and let baby peel them off. Pinch-peel requires precise finger coordination.
Count consistent words this week including approximations. Target: 10+ words by 15 months. Each is celebrated explicitly.
Listen for first two-word combinations: 'more doodh', 'mama up'. These typically appear 15–18 months and mark a major leap.
Extend body part naming to 5: naak, haath, paon, aankhein, kaan. Can baby point to each when named?
Point to pictures and ask 'What's this?' Wait. If no answer, name it and move on. No pressure: repeated exposure is what builds it.
Pick up the ball AND put it in the box.' Two-step unrelated instructions mark a significant receptive language leap.
Hold a wooden spoon to your ear: 'Hello? Yeh kaun hai?' Let baby take it. Symbolic play and communication combined.
When baby says 'ball', say 'ball (red ball) big round ball!' Each expansion teaches vocabulary and sentence structure simultaneously.
Sing a familiar song and pause before the last word of each line. Wait for baby to fill it in vocally or with gesture.
Baby feeds a doll, puts it to sleep, covers it with a cloth. Three-step pretend = narrative thinking beginning.
Give baby two identical cups and two identical spoons. Can they match the cups together and spoons together?
Materials Required: Two matching pairs of household objects

How To Do It: Hide a toy under one of two cups while baby watches. Swap the cups slowly. Which cup do they check? A-not-B error is normal now.
Place all red objects in one pile, all blue in another: demonstrate. Don't expect success yet; the repeated demonstration is the teaching.
During stacking or sorting, count aloud slowly: 'Ek, do, teen.' One-to-one counting comprehension comes later: hearing it is the start.
Offer a toy with multiple actions: press this to make sound, turn that to see movement. Systematic testing of each element is science.
Arrange play near another toddler. Don't expect interaction. Parallel play is the developmentally correct stage: don't rush sharing.
When a tantrum happens, narrate calmly: 'You're very frustrated. You wanted that and you can't have it. That's hard.' Name: don't fix.
When baby says 'mine', acknowledge the feeling: 'Yes, that's yours.' Teaching ownership feelings before teaching sharing.
If baby has a preferred toy or cloth, honour it. A comfort object is not a crutch: it is an autonomous self-regulation tool.
When baby achieves something, your response matters. Specific warm praise: 'You put all the blocks in! You worked hard at that.'
Create a safe floor space and let baby play alone for 5–10 minutes without intervention. Independent play is a skill to build.
Cooked spaghetti, wet sand, or yoghurt on a tray. Sensory tolerance for unfamiliar textures is built through repeated low-pressure exposure.
Walk outdoors and collect leaves, stones, sticks (safe). Back home, handle and sort them. Natural materials are rich sensory input.
Pots, wooden spoon, dried rice in a container. Make music together. Rhythm production is both sensory and fine motor.
Roll baby gently on the floor or spin slowly in arms. Vestibular input supports balance, posture, and regulation.
Knead some atta (wheat dough) together. Baby squeezes, pokes, and flattens. Playdough is pure fine motor and tactile input.
Encourage spoon use at every meal, however messy. Competence by 18 months is the target: not table manners, just the motor skill.
Ask baby to push their arm through a sleeve or lift a foot for a sock. Participation (however partial) builds independence.
Running at 16–18 months is stiff-legged but consistent. Give open safe space and let them run freely: don't slow them down.
Walk up stairs holding the rail, one hand held. Alternating feet on stairs typically appears around 2 years: step-together is fine now.
Set up a 'goal' (two objects as posts) and encourage kicking the ball between them. Directed kicking requires motor planning.
Stand baby on the bottom stair or a thick book. Encourage jumping off with both feet. Landing with both feet = motor milestone.
At a playground or safe homemade version, let baby climb up and come down a small slide. Height + movement = vestibular rich.
A push-along ride-on (or cardboard box to sit in) builds leg strength and spatial navigation before a true pedalling bike.
Materials Required: Ride-on toy or adapted cardboard box

How To Do It: Make a 'beam' with masking tape on the floor. Encourage walking along the line with arms out. Balance challenges in a safe context.
Ask baby to carry a small bag with a few books inside across the room. Heavy carrying is regulating to the sensory system.
Show drawing a horizontal line across paper and let baby try. Any deliberate directional mark is an achievement.
Practice opening and closing containers with twist lids. Rotation movements are a distinct fine motor skill used in daily life.
6-block tower requires spatial planning, grip calibration, and controlled release. Each additional block is harder than it looks.
Provide magazines or old newspaper for tearing. Bilateral tearing requires both hands working in opposition: a coordination milestone.
Thread 5 large beads or pasta pieces onto a shoelace. Requires visual targeting, bilateral coordination, and sustained attention.
A simple inset puzzle builds visual discrimination, spatial rotation, and the tolerance for trial-and-error failure.
By 18 months, 20–50 words (including approximations) is the developmental target. Under 10 words by 18 months warrants a paediatrician mention.
More doodh', 'bye dada', 'big ball.' Two-word phrases by 18 months are a major milestone. Model them in all conversation.
Baby will point at everything and say 'woh kya hai?' or similar. Every time: name it, describe it in one sentence, wait.
Tell a simple 3-sentence story about something that happened today. Story structure (beginning, middle, end) is absorbed before it is produced.
Kutte kya bolta hai? Bhow bhow!' Sound-to-animal linking builds vocabulary through a different encoding channel.
Focus on verbs this week: running, eating, sleeping, jumping. Action vocabulary is as important as noun vocabulary.
Same book, multiple days in a row. When baby anticipates a page, they are demonstrating memory, sequence, and language: simultaneously.
In familiar songs, pause on the last word of each line and wait. By 18 months many babies fill in the word: word retrieval practice.
Give baby pots, spoons, and empty containers. Let them 'cook.' Pretend play now represents real sequences observed in daily life.
Sort objects into two groups by shape: round things here, flat things there. Demonstrate; don't expect immediate success.
Show a picture of a cup, then ask baby to find the real cup. Picture-object correspondence is an abstract cognitive skill.
Begin a familiar routine and stop mid-way. Watch baby signal or try to complete it: sequence memory is confirming itself.
Place 1, then 2, then 3 objects in a line counting aloud as you do. One-to-one correspondence is being seeded; production comes later.
Tape a desirable toy lightly to a table or box. Watch how baby figures out removing the tape or pulling the object free.
When emotions arise, sit close and name the emotion specifically: 'You're angry. That felt unfair.' Don't fix: just name and stay.
Put a simple 4-face chart on the wall: happy, sad, angry, scared. 'How are you feeling today? Point to the face.' No judgment.
Develop a 3-step goodbye sequence for separations. Consistent, brief, warm: never long and uncertain. Consistency reduces distress.
Sit facing each other and roll a ball back and forth. Taking turns in a structured physical game is cooperative play emerging.
When a character in a book is sad or scared, narrate: 'Woh dara hua hai. Tum kya sochte ho?' Perspective-taking through story.
Let baby 'help' wipe a surface, stir food, hand you objects. Social participation and competence are both being built.
This month use a different fill each week: sand, water, dried beans, shredded paper. Sensory tolerance broadens with variety.
Walking barefoot on grass, sand, or dirt provides proprioceptive richness that shoes remove. 10 minutes barefoot outdoors = rich input.
Commercial clay or homemade atta dough. Squeezing, rolling, and flattening are pure fine motor with rich tactile feedback.
Make the same sound loudly and quietly: the same instrument or voice. Can baby identify louder and quieter? Auditory discrimination.
Roll baby gently in a blanket: not tight. The whole-body deep pressure is calming for the nervous system and delights most toddlers.
Offer fork for stabbing soft foods. Fork + spoon both available. Child chooses: autonomy in eating builds a positive food relationship.
Demonstrate hand washing before every meal and after outdoors. By 18 months, with reminding and help, this is beginning to establish.
Set up a simple course: run to the tree, run back. Direction change while running requires significant motor planning updates.
From ground level, encourage jumping with both feet simultaneously leaving the ground. Landing on both feet = major gross motor milestone.
Practice both directions on stairs with one hand on rail. Safety and independence are both being built.
Place a ball on the ground and ask baby to kick it. A stationary kick before a rolling ball: motor precision building.
Hold baby's hand and ask them to lift one foot for 2 seconds. Brief one-foot balance appearing 18–24 months.
Any safe climbing frame or jungle gym. Climbing is the most efficient builder of strength, coordination, and risk assessment.
Set up a large container and throw soft balls into it from a metre away. Aimed throwing builds visual-motor coordination.
Push-along ride-on with steerable wheels, or just steering a cart. Navigation and steering need practice just like walking did.
Show drawing a line from top to bottom and let toddler try. Directional mark-making is the direct precursor to letter formation.
Show drawing a circle slowly and let toddler try. Circle before straight lines: fine motor milestone at 24–27 months when it appears.
8-block tower requires sequential spatial planning: each level must be stable before the next. The planning IS the developmental work.
Introduce child-safe scissors with a parent steadying the paper. Cutting requires bilateral coordination and sustained grip.
Press pegs into a pegboard. Requires visual targeting, push force calibration, and the release of placing.
Lace a shoelace through large holes in cardboard. Pre-lacing builds the same hand movements as actual shoe-lacing later.
50+ words by 20 months is solid. Under 20 consistent words by 20 months is worth discussing with a paediatrician.
More apple please', 'Mama come here.' Three-word combinations beginning to appear 19–24 months.
Aryan do it!' Using own name before 'I' is developmentally normal and means self-concept is forming.
When toddler asks 'why' (it starts!), answer simply and then ask 'why do you think?' Turn every why into a conversation.
After reading a familiar book, close it and ask 'What happened?' Listen for any sequence: even one event recalled is narrative memory.
Introduce one colour per week. Label it consistently all week: 'The red cup. Your red shoes. Red tomatoes!' One at a time works best.
Pick up the cup AND bring it to me.' Two unrelated steps in sequence tests working memory as well as language.
Ask open questions about recent experiences: 'What did you see at the park?' Don't correct answers: expand and continue.
Stack 3 books then push: watch toddler's face. Set up a ramp and roll a ball down. Multi-step cause-effect chains are interesting now.
Use pictures or objects: sort animals from foods. Categorisation by function or type is a major cognitive leap.
After a routine, ask what comes next: 'We had bath. Then what? Then what?' Three-event sequence recall is emerging.
6–8 piece puzzle requiring rotation and trial-and-error. The frustration tolerance needed here is as developmental as the spatial skill.
Place 3 objects in a line and count them together: touch each as you count. One-to-one correspondence beginning to appear.
4 pairs of matching cards face-down. Turn over 2 at a time. Early working memory and concentration.
Before a frustrating task, name the strategy: 'If this is hard, take a breath.' Practice during calm so it is available during frustration.
Establish clear turn-taking in a simple game. 'Meri baari. Ab tumhari baari.' Consistent language makes the rule learnable.
Point out someone who is sad or hurt. 'Woh roh raha hai. Use dard hua. Hum kya kar sakte hain?' Empathy is taught through narration.
Set up a tea party or cooking scenario with dolls. Taking roles in pretend play is social cognition and narrative combined.
When toddler is upset, model the phrase: 'I don't like that' or 'Mujhe yeh pasand nahi.' Give them words for their feelings.
Introduce a simple self-comfort strategy in a calm moment: slow breathing, squeezing a soft object. Practice before it is needed.
Two containers of water, a cup for transferring. Supervised water play for 15 min. Pouring, splashing, and measuring emerge naturally.
Roll, flatten, and cut playdough with a blunt knife. Making shapes adds visual-motor control to the tactile input.
Walk outside and collect one of each: a leaf, a stone, a stick, a feather. Touch and describe each one together.
Blow bubbles and let toddler pop them. Tracking, reaching, timing, and the satisfying pop make this multi-sensory and motivating.
Finger painting (food-safe paint or safe craft paint). Each colour is introduced separately. Direct contact with material.
Name each clothing item as it goes on. Ask toddler to help push arm through sleeve or lift foot for shoe. Participation builds independence.
Brush teeth together at the same time. Letting toddler hold and attempt the brush first builds cooperation with the hygiene routine.
Set up household obstacles to run around: chairs, cushions, a line of tape. Navigating while running requires real-time motor planning.
Put a tape line on the floor. Jump over with both feet. Clearing an obstacle while jumping = significantly harder than jumping in place.
Practice walking backward, first holding hands then free. Backward locomotion requires body-awareness and spatial recalibration.
Roll a large ball back and forth, then graduate to low throwing and catching. Catching a rolling ball before a thrown one.
Practice on a tricycle or balance bike. Pedalling requires reciprocal leg movement: the same pattern as walking but with sustained force.
Demonstrate a gallop (lead-foot, drag) and encourage copying. Galloping before skipping: the intermediate coordination step.
Encourage alternating feet on the way up the stairs. May still need rail; alternating feet up is a 24–30 month milestone.
Encourage pushing a chair or pulling a loaded bag. Resistance exercise builds core strength and spatial navigation simultaneously.
Show a horizontal line (left to right) and ask child to copy. Directionality in drawing precedes directionality in writing.
Demonstrate a circle slowly and let child try. Circle-copying typically appears 24–30 months: earlier than + or V shapes.
Child-safe scissors: snip fringe into paper strips. Each snip is a complete bilateral motor action.
Pour water from a small jug into a cup. The control of flow is a daily self-care fine motor skill used for years.
8–10 piece puzzle requiring rotation and spatial reasoning. Systematically trying each piece before accepting failure is the cognitive goal.
Sort household objects into 3 colour groups. Naming the colours correctly while sorting combines language and cognition.
200 words by 24 months is the benchmark (CDC). Under 50 words by 24 months is worth professional discussion.
Mama, more water please.' Three-word phrases mark a significant vocabulary and grammar step appearing 21–24 months.
I want' and 'Give me' appearing means self-concept is strongly established. Model these forms throughout the day.
What happened at the park today?' Not 'Did you have fun?' Open questions require memory, sequencing, and language simultaneously.
During book reading, stop before a page turn: 'What do you think will happen next?' Prediction requires language plus narrative cognition.
Not a colour worksheet: just naming colours of real objects throughout the day. Context makes the association stronger.
Cat (bat) sat: mat!' Rhyming awareness at 24 months predicts reading readiness. Even partial awareness is worth celebrating.
At bedtime, ask child to tell you two things that happened today. This builds narrative language and episodic memory together.
Sort objects into two groups: big and small. Size concept develops through sorting, not worksheets.
Ask: 'What do we do after breakfast? Then what?' Three to four event sequence recall is the target at this age.
Build a simple colour or shape pattern: red, blue, red, blue, and leave a gap. Can child predict what comes next?
Pour water into an empty glass; let child pour it back. 'Full. Empty. Full again.' Concrete object manipulation precedes abstract concept.
Show baby photos of family members. Can child identify who it is? Memory across time = abstract object permanence.
Place 4 objects in a line; touch each as you count 1-2-3-4. Guide child's hand to touch each. Counting with meaning, not reciting.
During play: 'You have 4 blocks. Can you give me 2?' Guided sharing builds number concept alongside social skill.
Build something together: 'I put one block, you put one block.' Turn-taking in construction is cooperative play at its clearest.
Name 5 emotions accurately this week: happy, sad, angry, scared, excited. Emotional vocabulary directly predicts social competence.
Join child's pretend play and add a new element: 'The baby is sleeping: shall we sing her a lori?' Extending the narrative.
Teach a specific phrase for frustration: 'I need help' or 'Mujhe madad chahiye.' Practice during calm: not during the moment.
When child hurts or upsets another: 'What could you say? How do you think they felt?' Modelling, not forcing. Empathy precedes apology.
Walk barefoot on grass, sand, and smooth pavement on the same outing. Noticing the difference is the sensory lesson.
Add food colouring to water in clear cups and mix two together. Watching red + blue = purple is both science and sensory.
Pots, boxes, metal bowls: each makes a different sound. Let child experiment with what each material produces.
Press small objects into dough to make impressions. Roll thin snakes. Cut with blunt knife. Precision work in tactile medium.
Materials Required: Atta dough and objects to press

How To Do It: Wrap child in a heavy blanket on a lap. Deep pressure input is calming for the autonomic nervous system.
By 24 months: pull trousers up and down, remove shoes and socks, help with shirts. All with support: independence is incremental.
If interest appears: describe what toilet training involves. Let child see the process. No pressure: readiness signs should lead.
Encourage jumping forward from standing, landing on both feet. Distance of jump increases each week as leg strength grows.
A plank, a garden wall, or tape on the floor. Walk along without falling off. Balance on a narrow path is a 2.5-year skill.
Hold child's hand and encourage hopping on one foot. Even one hop is the milestone beginning: don't expect sustained hopping yet.
Bounce a large ball to child. Catching a bounced ball before a thrown one: the visual tracking time is longer.
Tricycle: practice steering around objects. Combining pedalling with directional control is a significant motor coordination step.
Move like different animals: frog jump, bear walk, crab walk, snake slither. Each uses different muscle groups and movement patterns.
Demonstrate an overhand throw and let child try. Overhand requires trunk rotation: a very different movement than underhand.
Help child do a forward roll on a soft surface. Head tuck, push-off, and landing = vestibular, motor, and spatial all together.
Show a + (cross) and let child try. Requires two directional lines crossing: harder than circle; appears around 30–36 months.
Fork for stabbing soft foods. The grip and stabbing force are different from a spoon: a distinct fine motor skill.
Button, zip, and dress a doll. This is fine motor practice that feels purposeful and maintains engagement longer.
Show folding a piece of paper in half and ask child to try. Aligning edges before folding requires spatial and motor precision.
Sort blocks by BOTH colour AND size together. Multi-attribute sorting is more demanding than single-attribute.
Materials Required: Blocks in multiple colours and sizes

How To Do It: Lace thread through holes to form a simple picture. Requires planning the sequence of holes to achieve the intended shape.
Ask child to tell a story about an animal they know. Even 2–3 sentences with a character is the emergence of narrative.
Why does it rain?' 'What would happen if…?' Complex question forms are emerging: answer simply and turn it back.
Consistent 3–4 word sentences with grammar: 'I want the red ball.' Grammar errors ('I goed') are developmentally correct now.
Does cat rhyme with bat? What about cat and dog?' Detecting rhyme before producing it: typical at 25–30 months.
Show a picture and ask 'What is happening here?' Child describes scene: vocabulary, grammar, and observation all combined.
Practice saying full name. 'What is your full name?' is a social comprehension milestone by age 3.
Have a 5-turn conversation where child asks at least one question. Asking is more advanced than answering.
After reading a favourite book many times, ask child to 'read' it to you from the pictures. Memory narrative is emerging.
Place up to 5 objects in a line and count together, touching each one. One-to-one correspondence solidifying now.
Big/small, hot/cold, fast/slow, loud/quiet. Opposites build comparative conceptual thinking.
Yesterday we went to the park. Today we are home.' Time concepts past/present solidify through consistent narration.
Sort objects into 4 groups: food, animals, clothes, vehicles. Four-category sorting is sophisticated categorical thinking.
Build red-blue-red-blue and leave a gap: 'What comes next?' Pattern extension requires holding the rule in working memory.
Here are 2 bananas. I add 1 more. How many now?' Concrete addition before abstract number.
If an imaginary friend appears, engage with them: 'What is their name?' Imaginary companions support language, emotional, and social development.
When a conflict arises over a toy: 'What could you offer them to trade?' Negotiation is a social skill that must be taught explicitly.
Create a display of child's achievements (drawings, photos). 'You did all of these!' Pride in accomplishment is a social-emotional milestone.
Set up a role-play scenario with simple props. Role-play at 25–30 months involves taking on another's perspective.
When feelings escalate, say 'Let's take a pause' and model slow breathing together. Practice before it is needed.
While reading or in real life: 'How do you think she felt when that happened?' Perspective-taking practice.
Tear and paste coloured tissue paper onto card. Tearing texture, paper texture, and glue texture are layered sensory inputs.
Watering can, puddles, or garden tap. Child-directed water exploration is rich sensory and cause-effect play.
Gather 8 objects of varied texture. Sort into 'rough' and 'smooth.' Tactile discrimination is now a language + sensory task.
Carrying loaded backpack, pushing a box of books, pulling a weighted trolley. Heavy work regulates the nervous system.
Spin with arms out, stop, try to stay balanced. Vestibular system input: intentional dizziness and recovery is regulating.
Let child brush their own teeth first, then parent finishes. Agency in the sequence builds cooperation with the hygiene routine.
If signs of readiness present (knowing when wet, interest in toilet), begin with simple potty introduction. Never forced.
From one hop, build to 3–5 consecutive hops on the same foot. Each hop requires rebalancing: rapid balance adjustment developing.
Most children gallop at 2.5 years and skip at 3.5. Practice gallop leading with each foot as the precursor.
Graduate from bounced to thrown ball catching. Tracking the trajectory and adjusting arms = complex visual-motor planning.
On a tricycle: practice pedalling and stopping at a marked line. Braking intentionally requires coordinated leg action.
Climbing a ladder (alternating hands and feet) is the most complex locomotion pattern children this age attempt.
Jump off a 30-cm step with both feet landing together. Judging safe heights and landing = spatial and motor cognition combined.
Walk a balance beam (tape line) with eyes closed for 2 steps. Eyes-closed balance challenges proprioceptive system intensely.
Chase game where child must dodge around obstacles. Reactive motor planning: responding to unexpected changes in a path.
Show a V and ask child to copy. Angular shapes (V, then +, then triangle) appear in sequence after circle.
Ask child to draw a person. Head + one other body part by 30 months = fine motor and representational thinking combined.
Cut along a straight line drawn on paper. Staying on the line requires visual monitoring while maintaining bilateral grip.
Peel self-adhesive stickers and place on a target. Two-stage finger action requiring precise coordination.
Demonstrate placing a block across two towers and ask child to build the same. Copying spatial models = architecture thinking.
Small beads on a thin lace. Fine pincer control plus visual targeting plus threading = high-demand fine motor task.
A 30-month-old typically has 450–600 words. Importantly, sentences are 3–5 words with mostly correct grammar.
Once there was a dog. He was hungry. He found some food and ate it.' Three-part narrative structure is the target.
I'm tired because I didn't sleep.' 'If it rains, we'll stay inside.' Logical connectors mark a grammar milestone.
How does a tap work?' Let child explain from their own understanding. Explanatory language is emerging.
I say cat: you say something that rhymes.' Production (not just detection) of rhymes = phonological awareness step.
Recognise the first letter of own name in print. This is enough letter knowledge to celebrate at 30 months.
Materials Required: Paper with child's name in large letters

How To Do It: What would you do if it was raining and you wanted to go outside?' Hypothetical thinking + language combined.
Retell a favourite story from memory using the book's pictures as prompts. 3-event sequence is the typical recall at this age.
Count 10 objects touching each one. At 30 months, 10-object counting with one-to-one correspondence is an achievable goal.
Are these the same or different?: with objects that are clearly one or the other. Comparative language + cognition.
Materials Required: Pairs of matching and non-matching objects

How To Do It: Group things that you eat, things you wear, things you sit on. Sorting by function is more abstract than sorting by appearance.

Activity Name: Spatial Concepts: In, On, Under, Behind
How To Do It: Put the cup on the book. Now under the book.' Following spatial prepositions in sequence.
What do we do in the morning? What happens in the evening?' Time-of-day sequencing before days of the week.
While reading: 'Why is the bear sad?': answer not in the text but inferrable from pictures. Early inferential thinking.
Facilitate play in a group of 3. Children this age can begin brief cooperative interaction: note who initiates and who follows.
Mujhe gussa aa raha hai' or 'I feel scared.' Verbal emotion expression before or instead of physical expression.
When a younger child needs help with something child can do: 'Can you show them how to stack the blocks?' Pro-social seed.
Offer 3 activities and let child choose. 'What would you like to do first?' Autonomous choice builds decision-making.
When something doesn't happen as planned, narrate: 'You're disappointed. That was important to you. Let's think about what we can do.'
Is it fair that she got 3 and you got 2?' Fairness reasoning appears at 2.5 years and is important to take seriously.
Mix cornstarch and water: it's both solid and liquid. Scientifically bizarre sensory experience. Let child explore freely.
Walk outside listening only: no talking. Point at sounds. Back home, draw or describe what you heard. Auditory attention focus.
Ice cubes in a bin of warm water. Feeling both together, watching ice melt. Temperature + observation + language.
Teach 3 simple yoga poses: tree, mountain, downward dog. Proprioceptive + balance + breath awareness combined.
Let child spin a top and watch. The visual tracking of a spinning object is uniquely absorbing at this age.
Pour their own water from a small child-sized jug into a cup at meals. Independence in self-care + fine motor + self-regulation.
Carry plates, fold napkins, place cutlery. Table-setting is fine motor + sequencing + contribution to family life.
Sustained hopping on one foot: first dominant then non-dominant. Non-dominant hopping develops several months after dominant.
Mark a starting line with tape. Jump forward as far as possible, both feet together. Measure distance: it increases weekly.
Tape a target circle on the wall at chest height. Throw a soft ball to hit it. Aimed at a vertical target = new motor challenge.
Pedal fast when you say go, slow when you say stop. Speed regulation while pedalling requires real-time motor control.
Backward walking on a balance beam (tape line): balance plus motor sequencing in an unusual direction.
A full obstacle course: run, jump over, crawl under, balance on, throw at. Complex movement sequence requiring memory of order.
Throw a ball, run to get it, throw again. Sequencing two motor actions with a transition tests motor working memory.
Lift knees high and march in time to music. Rhythmic bilateral motor coordination and gross motor control.
Square (4 equal sides, 4 corners) is harder than a circle: requires direction changes at precise points. Appears ~33–36 months.
Head, eyes, arms, legs. Drawing a person with 4 identifiable features is a 3-year representational drawing milestone.
After mastering straight-line cutting, introduce a curve to cut along. Following a curve requires continuous adjustment.
Demonstrate and let child practice buttoning a shirt or coat with large buttons. Fine pincer + hand-eye coordination.
Materials Required: Shirt or coat with large buttons

How To Do It: Weave paper strips over and under to make a simple mat. The alternating pattern requires sustained visual-motor tracking.
Trace the letters of own name with a finger, then crayon. Letter tracing before writing = spatial learning of letter forms.
By 33 months, vocabulary typically 700–900 words with 5–6 word sentences used consistently.
Follow a chain of 'why' questions: 'Why does it rain?' → 'Because the clouds get heavy.' → 'Why do they get heavy?' Sustain 3 turns.
Red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, black, white. Naming all basic colours correctly is a 3-year language milestone.
Two dogs, three cats.' Plural '-s' rule solidifying. Point out examples: 'Look: two birds. Birds: more than one.'
I walked. We played. She jumped.' Regular past tense (-ed) appearing. Irregular past ('went', 'ran') still developing.
Tell me everything you see in this picture.' Descriptive language drill: vocabulary, grammar, and observation combined.
If we water the plant, it will grow.' If-then reasoning expressed in language: logical thinking made verbal.
Introduce 3 letter sounds: 'A says ah, B says bah, M says mah.' Sound-letter pairs before letter names: phonics groundwork.
Extend counting to 15 objects with one-to-one correspondence. Counting past 10 requires learning the teen number pattern.
Circle, square, triangle, rectangle, oval. Naming all 5 basic shapes by name = geometry milestone at 33 months.
Place 3 objects here and 5 there. 'Which group has more?' Comparative quantity: not counting, but visual quantity judgement.
6 matching pairs face-down. Turn 2, find matches. Working memory and concentration targeted directly.
4 story pictures out of order. Can child arrange them in logical sequence? Narrative + causal reasoning combined.
Line up 3 objects. 'Which is first? Last? Middle?' Ordinal position language builds mathematical foundation.
Who is your friend? What do you like about them?' Friendship awareness at 31–33 months is a social milestone.
Play a group game with 3–4 children where turns rotate. Supporting turn-taking in a group is more complex than in a pair.
When a request must be declined, practice accepting it with words: 'Okay, maybe later.' Delayed gratification is teachable.
Two people draw on the same paper at the same time. Sharing a creative space without conflict is social maturity.
Materials Required: Large paper and crayons for two

How To Do It: Dadi looks tired today. What do you think she needs?' Reading real (not illustrated) emotional states is a harder skill.
When another child is upset: 'Can you think of something that might help them feel better?' Pro-social action seeded.
Outdoors: soil, water, pots, spoons. Make 'food', serve it, clean up. Sensory + imaginative + gross + fine motor all together.
In bright sunlight, make and change shadow shapes. Tracing shadows on paper. Visual perception + fine motor + science.
A magnet and various household objects. Which ones stick? Systematic testing of a material property.
Clap a 3-beat pattern and ask child to copy. Grade to 4-beat. Rhythmic working memory and motor sequencing.
Blindfold or closed eyes; feel an object and name it. Tactile recognition without visual aid.
Peel a banana, spread butter on toast, pour cereal. Contributing to own food preparation builds self-care and agency.
By 33 months: pull trousers up/down, put on shoes (even wrong feet), put on hat, take off jacket. Independence in sequence.
True skipping (step-hop alternating feet) typically appears 3.5–4 years. Practice the step-hop on each foot separately first.
Tennis-ball-sized throw and catch at 2 metres. Smaller ball demands greater precision than large-ball catching.
10+ consecutive hops on the preferred foot. Non-preferred foot at this stage is typically 5–8 hops.
Mark two lines 40 cm apart. Jump from one to the other with both feet. Distance increases as leg strength and timing improve.
5-second one-foot balance without support. Practice eyes open then eventually eyes closed.
Bounce and catch a ball repeatedly. Dribbling (bouncing without catching) is harder and typically 4–5 years.
Move to the beat of different musical styles. Rhythmic entrainment (body movement matching musical tempo) is a motor milestone.
Gallop while holding an object in one hand. Dual-task motor automatisation: galloping becomes automatic enough for a second task.
Triangle requires three directional line changes at precise angles. Typically appearing 36 months: harder than square.
Head, body, 2 arms, 2 legs. By 36 months: 6-part person is the benchmark drawing milestone.
Trace each letter of first name carefully. Letter-form learning happens through the motor movement, not just visual recognition.
Cut out a simple shape (circle or triangle) drawn on paper. Following curved and angular lines in cutting.
Fold a piece of paper in thirds and tuck in the edges to make a simple envelope. Spatial folding and precise crease-making.
Build a house, bridge, or tower using a picture as a model. Copying a 3D structure from a 2D picture is abstract spatial cognition.
At 36 months, vocabulary typically 900–1200 words. Strangers should understand 75–100% of speech by this age.
After reading a book, ask child to retell it in order without pictures. 4-event sequence recall is the 3-year target.
Yesterday I played. Tomorrow we will go.' Past and future tense correct usage is a 3-year grammar milestone.
Why does the ball roll? Why does the fan spin?' 3-year-olds begin to explain mechanisms, not just name them.
What sound does S make? Dog starts with what letter?' 5-letter sound associations by 36 months = strong phonics foundation.
The big red dog ran away.' Complex sentences with adjectives and adverbs consistently = strong language development.
Is a cat or a dog better to have? Why?' Opinion + justification: the beginning of argument and persuasive language.
Cat, bat, sat, hat, rat: all rhyme. What else rhymes with cat?' Generating rhymes from a family = phonological fluency.
Count 20 objects one-to-one. Past 12, children must remember the teen pattern; past 20, the decade pattern begins.
How many elephants are on this table? Zero. Zero means none.' Zero as a quantity is an abstract concept to teach explicitly.
Red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, pink, black, white, brown. Naming all 10 basic colours by 36 months is solid.
Sing or say days of the week in sequence. Memorising the sequence before understanding the concept: sequence comes first.
AABB pattern: red, red, blue, blue, red, red… 'What comes next?' Two-repeat pattern is harder than ABAB.
Why did that happen? What caused it?' Causal explanation (not just observation but mechanism) is a 3-year cognitive goal.
Play a simple game with explicit rules (ludo, snap). Following rules in a game is the first social contract: a major SE milestone.
Teach: 'Stop. Think. Speak.' When a conflict happens, model the steps: pause, consider the other person, use words.
I notice your face looks cross. Are you feeling frustrated before it comes out big?' Self-awareness before dysregulation.
I'm sorry I took your toy. I know that made you sad.' Empathy embedded in apology: what they did + how the other felt.
Practice in a real game. Celebrate both: 'You lost this time and stayed kind. That is very hard and very mature.'
Who is your favourite person to play with? What do you do together?' Intentional friendship at 3 is a social milestone.
I know you want it now. Let's wait 2 minutes together.' Practise with a timer. Delayed gratification is a teachable executive function.
Mix glue and bicarbonate of soda (or contact lens solution). Unique tactile input: stretchy, gooey, satisfying. Full sensory engagement.
Materials Required: PVA glue, bicarbonate of soda, contact lens solution

How To Do It: Walk a route where child closes eyes at each stop and describes what they hear and feel. One sense at a time, deliberately.
Press leaves, bark, or flowers with paint onto paper. The texture transfer is visual, tactile, and creative simultaneously.
Feel objects in a bag without looking. Name or describe them. Pure tactile recognition with language challenge added.
Assign different percussion sounds to different family members. Create a rhythm piece together. Auditory + motor + social.
Wake, toilet, wash face, brush teeth, dress: child does as much as possible. Independence in sequence, not perfection in execution.
Set the table, put laundry in the basket, water a plant. Contributing to household function builds competence and belonging.
Skip from one end of the room to the other. Alternate leading foot each trip. Distance and coordination both increase weekly.
Gallop to a point, pick up an object, gallop back. Combining a motor skill with a task = motor automatisation.
Increase throwing distance to 3 metres. Overhand distance throw = full shoulder rotation and trunk twist working together.
After mastering dominant foot hopping, work on non-dominant. Often takes 3–6 months more than dominant foot.
Teach the leg-pump rhythm for swinging independently. Pendulum mechanics + body coordination + rhythm = rich learning.
Hold rope and jump over it laid flat, then swing it slowly. Full jump rope is 5–6 years; foundations built from 3 years.
Catch a large soft ball with one hand. Single-hand catching requires much faster visual-motor processing than two-hand.
Navigate around cones or objects at speed. Complex steering + speed control.
Diamond shape = two triangles. More complex than triangle; appears 4–5 years. Begin exploring it with guided tracing.
First attempt at unaided name writing. Any recognisable letters = progress. Letter formation before order: order comes second.
Build a paper crown, collage, or model from 4+ steps with different materials. Planning and sequencing a multi-material project.
Measure objects with a ruler: 'This book is 20 centimetres long.' Combining numeracy with fine motor tool use.
Fold paper boat or simple origami frog. 4–5 creases requiring precise spatial awareness and planning.
Demonstrate and let child attempt braiding 3 ribbons or cords. The over-under-over pattern is executive function in the hands.
Spontaneous storytelling with a character, a problem, 3 events, and a resolution. Narrative structure growing.
Sustain a chain of why-question-and-answer 3 turns deep. Each answer must be a full sentence.
Introduce the alphabet song. Letter names before letter sounds: the song is a memory sequence, not phonics yet.
Tell me 5 things you did yesterday.' Episodic memory recall + narrative sequencing in combination.
The dog ran AND the cat hid.' Compound sentences (two clauses joined by 'and', 'but', 'so') are a grammar milestone.
-at words: cat, bat, sat, mat, hat.' Word families build phonological pattern recognition.
5-turn conversation with an unfamiliar adult. Sustaining conversation with non-family adults = social language milestone.
Read familiar logos, signs, and labels in the environment: shop name, cereal box, road signs. Environmental print = first reading.
3 bananas + 2 bananas = 5 bananas.' Concrete object addition. The concept of adding before the symbol.
5 blocks. Take away 2. How many left?' Concrete subtraction. Count what remains, not just recite the answer.
Which stick is longer? Which cup holds more?' Direct comparison measurement before formal units.
Sing and recite days of the week in order. Mark each day on a simple calendar together.
More complex pattern: red, red, blue, blue, green. 5-element pattern before repeating: demands higher working memory.
Draw a simple map of one room together. Spatial representation (map making) is abstract spatial cognition beginning.
Build something together that neither could build alone: a fort, a long train, a tall tower. True cooperation with shared goal.
Act out a common conflict and try different resolutions. Role-playing the resolution builds the script for real situations.
How big are your feelings? A little bit or a LOT?' Emotion intensity awareness before intensity regulation.
What shall we do this afternoon? What do we need? What should we do first?' Child-led planning with support.
Your friend likes climbing. You like painting. Both are great.' Differences in preference as valid and interesting: not better/worse.
When a friend achieves something: 'How do you feel about what they did? Can you tell them?' Pro-social emotion building.
Make something from clay without a model or prompt. Imagination into 3D form: high-level creative and fine motor combined.
Draw a map of sounds heard in the house: kitchen sounds, garden sounds. Audio representation in a visual medium.
Collect 10 different textures (sandpaper, foil, fabric, bark) and stick on card. The making and the touching are both the activity.
Involve child in making a simple dish: pancake batter, lemonade. Measuring, pouring, mixing = sensory + numeracy + fine motor.
Let's take 3 big breaths together. In through the nose, out through the mouth.' Begin building breath as a self-regulation tool.
Full dress sequence independently except challenging fastenings. Independence in self-care is as developmental as any skill.
Pour cereal, peel banana, spread butter on toast. Self-feeding preparation builds agency, fine motor, and self-reliance.
Skip, then on a signal change direction. Changing a skill mid-execution is a high-level motor planning task.
Kick a ball rolled toward them: timing a kick to a moving target is significantly harder than kicking a stationary one.
Hop across a room on one foot: 5+ metres. Distance hopping builds stamina as well as motor control.
Walk backward along a tape line without stepping off. Backward balance beam requires proprioceptive awareness.
Run at full speed to a point when they hear 'go', slow to a jog on 'slow.' Speed modulation on command.
Catching a tennis-ball-sized object thrown from 2 m with two hands closing at the right moment.
Begin learning to turn a short rope independently and jump. Step over first, then small jumps, then rhythmic jumping.
Step-slide-step sideways in both directions. Lateral movement uses a different motor pattern from forward locomotion.
Write first and last name initials without tracing. Letter formation from memory, not visual copying.
Stick small squares of coloured paper onto a grid to make a pattern. Precision placement in a constrained space.
Materials Required: Small coloured squares, grid paper, glue

How To Do It: Supervised stapler use. Knowing the correct pressure and position = tool awareness and fine motor calibration.
Cut along a zig-zag line. Directional change while cutting is harder than cutting a curve.
Weave cloth strips over and under cardboard loom slots. Over-under alternation sustained across a whole piece.
Thread large-eyed blunt needle and make running stitch on open-weave fabric. Tactile + fine motor + sequencing.
At 3y6m, vocabulary is typically 1200–1500 words. Sentences are 5–6 words with complex grammar emerging.
Say a sentence; child repeats, then writes it with whatever letters they know. Any attempt that maps to the sentence is progress.
Cat, sat, mat, big, fit. Sound-blending 3-letter words: c-a-t = cat. The first reading bridge.
I was cold, SO I put on a jumper.' Complex clause connectors = significant grammar sophistication.
How do you make a sandwich? Tell me each step.' Procedural language: sequenced instruction giving.
When communication breaks down, teach: 'I don't understand: can you say it a different way?' Repair is advanced pragmatic skill.
Daily 'news' time: 'Tell me one important thing that happened today.' Selective recall + reporting = executive + language.
A 3-clue picture crossword. Name the picture, count letters, fill boxes. Reading + counting + writing combined.
Here are 4 blocks. I give you 3 more. How many altogether?' Count all strategy: touching each object to count.
Remove objects from a group and count what remains. Cover the removed objects so child counts only remaining.

Activity Name: Name Days of Week in Order
How To Do It: Recite days of week reliably in order. Begin linking days to events: 'On Monday we have swimming.'
Name 4 seasons and one characteristic of each. 'Winter is cold. Summer is hot.' Concept before observation.
Sort 20 objects into 3 groups. Count each group. Draw a simple bar graph of the results. Data literacy beginning.
Is a dog living? Is a chair living?' Living/non-living is the first science classification concept.
I feel like I need a break before I get too frustrated.' Body-awareness + self-advocacy + language = emotional executive function.
You want X, I want Y. What if we do X for 10 minutes and then Y?' Compromise as a concept explicitly taught.
Tell me 5 things about you.' Not what you do: who you are. Self-concept building is the 3-year social-emotional task.
Your friend seems quiet today. What could you do?' Friendship requires maintenance actions: teach them explicitly.
You're disappointed. Let's say what you're feeling and think of one thing that might help.' Disappointment skill.
Name 3 things you're grateful for at dinner. Gratitude practice correlates with wellbeing and prosocial behaviour.
Make chapati or simple bread together. Feel dough, smell cooking, hear sizzle, taste result. All 5 senses in one activity.
Fill ice trays with water + small objects. Freeze. Let child unmelt at room temperature or with warm water. Science + sensory.
Weave grass, leaves, and twigs through a simple frame. Outdoor sensory + fine motor + creativity.
Sit quietly for 2 minutes. When timer rings, share 3 things you heard. Auditory attention + metacognition.
In a darkened room, explore light through coloured acetate or water. Light science + visual sensory exploration.
Materials Required: Torch, coloured acetate or water in bag

How To Do It: Wake, toilet, wash, dress, breakfast: child completes the entire sequence with minimal reminders. Executive function in action.
One daily chore owned completely: watering a plant, setting the table, feeding a pet. Responsibility + competence.
Jump over a rolling ball. Timing a jump to a moving target is a higher motor planning demand than a stationary jump.
Bounce a ball continuously while walking, then while running. Dual-task automatisation: locomotion + ball control.
8-second one-foot balance, eyes open. Begin introducing eyes-closed versions briefly.
Forward roll without assistance. Head tuck, push-off, round-back landing. Proprioception and vestibular combined.
Walk heel-to-toe in a straight line, arms out. Tandem walking tests balance in a constrained path.
Gallop to music, matching the tempo. Rhythmic locomotion: motor planning linked to auditory input.
Underhand toss into a basket from 1.5 m. Underhand vs overhand uses different arm mechanics -- both need practice.
Demonstrate jumping jacks and let child try. Coordinating arm and leg movement simultaneously -- hard at this age.
Correct formation of letters A, B, C, D, E. Top-to-bottom and left-to-right directional habits built now last a lifetime.
Paint with watercolours, rinsing brush between colours. Controlling dilution and brush pressure = fine motor calibration.
Simple over-under weaving on a cardboard loom. Alternating the direction of each row = pattern thinking in the hands.
Punch holes along the edge of paper to make a lacing card. Using a hole punch requires significant grip force.
Draw a spiral and cut along the line. The continuously changing direction is the most demanding cutting challenge yet.
Roll clay into a long thin snake without breaking it. Fine pressure calibration -- too hard = flatten, too soft = break.
Read 3-word sentences: 'The cat sat.' Sound each letter, blend. First independent reading = a landmark moment.
Materials Required: Simple reader or card with sentences

How To Do It: Write simple consonant-vowel-consonant words: cat, sit, big. Encoding = higher skill than decoding. Celebrate any attempt.
The small brown dog ran quickly.' Describe objects and actions with modifiers -- vocabulary sophistication growing.
Learn one simple joke and tell it to someone. Jokes require understanding that words can have two meanings -- abstract language.
Read a short paragraph, then ask: 'What was it about? Say it in two sentences.' Summarising requires comprehension + language.
Common sight words: the, and, is, it, in, on, a, I, to, he. Sight word reading is memory + print awareness.
Tell me how to get to the kitchen from here.' Spatial language + perspective-taking + sequential instruction.
Some people think dogs are better than cats. Some think cats are better. What's your view? Why?' Beginning of argument.
Concrete then pictorial then symbolic. '4+3=?' on paper, with objects to count if needed.
2, 4, 6 are even -- can be split into two equal groups. 1, 3, 5 cannot. Concrete splitting before the rule.
Recite months in order. Link each to a family event: 'My birthday is in July.' Sequence then meaning.
Identify coins by appearance and name their values. Sorting coins by value -- not yet purchasing, just denominations.
What do plants need? What do animals need?' Beginning biology -- organisms have requirements for survival.
A map of the house or garden. Find a 'treasure' hidden using map coordinates. Spatial representation reading.
Wait 5 minutes for something desirable with a visible timer. Narrate the wait: 'We're waiting. That is hard. We can do it.'
Practice saying 'I need...' or 'Can I have...' instead of grabbing, whining, or melting down. Verbal request habit.
Before I say what I want, let me notice how you are feeling.' Other-first awareness is sophisticated SE development.
Read a book about a character who faces difficulty and succeeds. Discuss: 'What did they do when it was hard?'
I think it's different because...' Teaching disagreement that doesn't damage the relationship.
Dictate a thank-you to someone who helped them. Gratitude expressed externally = prosocial behaviour building.
Mix baking soda and vinegar in a bowl. Watch, discuss why it fizzes. Hypothesis before result -- early science thinking.
Blindfolded: smell 6 household items and name them. Olfactory discrimination is rarely directly exercised.
Make hand-shadow animals on a wall with a torch. Visual creation + fine motor + narrative.
Clap a 4-beat pattern and ask child to copy. Then let them create one for you to copy. Rhythmic working memory.
Plant a seed and draw it each week. Observation + recording + science concept of growth over time.
Child packs their own bag with a checklist: water bottle, lunch, library book, uniform. Executive function daily practice.
Your responsibility: water bottle goes in your bag, shoes go in the rack, toys go in the box.' Ownership of own items.
Skip to a point, pick up an object, skip back -- in competition with self (timer) or family. Speed + skill combined.
Balance on tiptoes for 10 seconds. Calf strength + balance + body awareness.
Overhand throw at a target 3 m away. Accuracy + distance combined = complex motor planning.
Any improvised wobble surface (cushion on board). Dynamic balance is harder than static balance.
Parent holds legs; child walks on hands. Shoulder girdle strength and weight-bearing through arms.
Run up and down stairs (safely). Requires much faster motor planning and leg activation than walking on stairs.
Dribble a ball around objects placed at 50-cm intervals. Controlled directional dribbling.
Jump from 40 cm and land softly -- bent knees, arms out. Controlled landing is as important as the jump itself.
Correct formation of letters F, G, H, I, J. Focus on correct starting point and direction.
Running stitch on open-weave fabric with a large blunt needle. Threading + in-out pattern + sustained fine motor.
Simple origami: bird or boat using 3-4 folds. Spatial + fine motor + following sequence.
Tie an overhand knot in a rope. Pre-cursor to shoe-tying. Loop and through.
Draw something that has never existed.' Imagination into representation -- no reference, only internal image.
Look at a photo or drawing of a structure and recreate it with blocks. 2D-to-3D translation.
Level-appropriate early reader: 8-12 pages, 1-2 sentences per page. Independent reading attempt.
3-5 words, own spelling attempt. 'The cat is big.' Phonetic spelling -- celebrate all attempts regardless of accuracy.
How did you know it was a dog? What told you?' Metacognitive language: explaining reasoning, not just answering.
Show-and-tell: choose an object and speak about it for 1 minute to family. Public speaking practice in a safe context.
Child interviews a parent or grandparent: 'What was your favourite food as a child?' Language + social + inquiry.
It's raining cats and dogs -- does that mean real cats and dogs?' Figurative language awareness beginning.
Fold 4 sheets of paper, staple, write a title, draw 4 pictures, dictate the story text. Author identity building.
Why do you think that? What makes you sure?' Adding evidence to an opinion. Critical thinking through language.
Extend arithmetic to 20 with concrete supports first. Count-on strategy: start from the larger number.
Materials Required: 20 objects + number line drawn on paper

How To Do It: Cut an apple or paper into 2 equal halves, then 4 equal quarters. Fraction concept through direct physical splitting.
Balance two objects on a plank over a pivot. Which is heavier? Direct comparison before scales.
How long is 1 minute? 5 minutes? Time a minute of activity, then wait a minute. Duration concept before clock reading.
Sort animals into mammals, birds, fish, insects. Classification by shared characteristics = taxonomy thinking.
Do you prefer apples or oranges?' Survey 5 family members, record results, draw graph. Data collection at its simplest.
When something seems unfair: 'Tell me what you think happened and what you think would be fair.' Reasoning about justice.
When playing with others: 'Is there anyone who isn't playing? Can we include them?' Proactive inclusivity.
Attempt something just beyond current ability for 5 minutes without giving up. 'I can't do it yet -- not yet.'
I'm bored.' Response: 'Let's see what you can create with these 5 things.' Resourcefulness from boredom = creativity.
What kinds of things make you feel very upset? Let's make a list.' Trigger awareness before trigger management.
